A position-only seam ($C^0$) that leaves a velocity step demands ideal acceleration impulses $\delta(t)$, which no physical actuator can deliver. Even when positions and velocities are matched ($C^1$), an unconstrained acceleration jump $\Delta\ddot{q}$ across the seam demands an instantaneous step change in electromagnetic torque $\Delta\tau = J_{\text{eff}} \Delta\ddot{q}$. Such torque changes can excite flexible transmission modes and increase wear; their consequences depend on magnitude, repetition, damping, and the drive response. @Fig-11-action-chunk-seam-continuity places that request beside its remedy, a finite $C^2$ bridge that removes the reference velocity step.

Carrying a full mug makes the role of acceleration changes tangible. Speed alone does not predict spilling: acceleration, jerk, cup geometry, and liquid motion all matter. In a rigid-inertia joint model, an acceleration step demands a torque step ($\tau = J_{\text{eff}}a$); the physical response depends on the drive and flexible structure. Enforcing $C^2$ continuity removes reference acceleration steps across segment boundaries, while bounding **jerk**\index{Jerk!definition} ($j=\dot a=\dddot x$) limits how rapidly that acceleration changes. Neither property alone guarantees payload retention or transmission life.

::: {#fig-11-action-chunk-seam-continuity fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Seam demand and checked bridge**: A position-matched velocity step creates a large one-tick inertial torque *request*. A finite $C^2$ bridge removes the reference velocity step, but its interior jerk, torque, and joint response still require validation." fig-alt="Panel (a) shows a velocity step at a trajectory seam and a high one-tick torque request. Panel (b) shows a smoother C-squared reference bridge. The diagram compares proposed reference demands, not measured torque."}
![](images/svg/fig11_action_chunk_seam_continuity.svg){width="100%"}
:::

::: {#dfn-planning-c-jerk-spline-seam .callout-definition title="C² spline seam"}

A ***$C^2$ spline seam***\index{C2 spline seam@$C^2$ spline seam!definition} is a trajectory junction that enforces continuity through the second time derivative (position, velocity, and acceleration) between adjoining motion segments.

1.  **Significance**: Prevents instantaneous acceleration steps across trajectory chunks, bounding the inertial torque spike $\tau_{\text{step}} = J_{\text{eff}} \Delta\ddot{q}$ demanded from actuators.
2.  **Distinction**: Distinct from $C^1$ continuity (which matches position and velocity but permits acceleration jumps) and $C^0$ continuity (which matches position but can leave a velocity step).
3.  **Common pitfall**: Assuming $C^2$ continuity guarantees torque feasibility; while acceleration is continuous, interior velocities, accelerations, or jerks within the blending bridge may still violate physical actuator or clearance limits.

:::

The transmission shapes the response to what the drive delivers. For a two-inertia model with load inertia $J_L$, reflected motor inertia $J_{\text{ref}}=N_g^2J_{\text{rotor}}$ (@sec-body-actuator-limits), and coupling stiffness $k_\theta$, the antiresonance and resonance frequencies of this model [@li2024optimal] are $\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{k_\theta/J_L}$ and $\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{k_\theta(1/J_L+1/J_{\text{ref}})}$. In the arm's strain-wave joints, reflected rotor inertia and a compliant transmission can amplify a sharp reference change, so admission needs the joint's identified, load-dependent modes and checks bridge extrema, torque, and drive limits against them. No frequency, stiffness, or jerk range transfers between products without measured parameters.[^fn-rule-servo-bandwidth]

### Quintic spline synthesis for C$^2$ boundary matching {#sec-planning-quintic-splines}

Smoothing the seam's velocity step requires online $C^2$ trajectory spline blending\index{C2 trajectory spline blending@$C^2$ trajectory spline blending}, which must be treated as the synthesis of an entirely new motion plan rather than as cosmetic filtering. When the planner inserts a polynomial bridge $\theta_{\mathrm{blend}}(t)$ over a transition interval $T_{\mathrm{blend}}$, a duration distinct from the blend deadline $t_{\mathrm{blend}}$, to connect chunk $A$ and incoming chunk $B$, the resulting bridge segment must undergo the exact same dynamic feasibility checks as the primary chunks.[^fn-hw-jerk-limits]

A local bridge must match position, velocity, and acceleration at two independently specified endpoints. A cubic has only four coefficients and cannot generally satisfy all six conditions; the quintic below has six. This local construction differs from fitting a globally continuous cubic spline across a batch of knots.

[^fn-hw-jerk-limits]: **Trajectory jerk**\index{Jerk!minimization}\index{Drivetrain!torsional resonance}: A jerk objective can make a particular bridge smoother. A finite jerk bound alone does not exclude energy near a measured resonance; the complete command spectrum and closed-loop response must be checked for the joint and load.

[^fn-rule-servo-bandwidth]: **Sampling and mechanical modes**\index{Bandwidth!servo sampling}: A control period faster than a mechanical mode can help resolve that mode but is not a stability proof. Controller stability latency margin, sensor delay, damping, filtering, and actuator bandwidth must be validated for the identified joint.

The bridge is a fifth-order (quintic) polynomial because torque follows acceleration ($\tau = J_{\mathrm{eff}}\ddot\theta$ in the rigid-inertia model), so a bridge that matches only velocity still leaves an acceleration step, and with it a torque step of $J_{\mathrm{eff}}\Delta\ddot\theta$. For $C^2$ continuity across the seam, the bridge must match position, velocity, and acceleration at both endpoints, a total of six boundary conditions:
$$\theta(0) = \theta_0, \quad \dot{\theta}(0) = \dot{\theta}_0, \quad \ddot{\theta}(0) = \ddot{\theta}_0$$
$$\theta(T_{\mathrm{blend}}) = \theta_1, \quad \dot{\theta}(T_{\mathrm{blend}}) = \dot{\theta}_1, \quad \ddot{\theta}(T_{\mathrm{blend}}) = \ddot{\theta}_1$$
where $(\theta_0, \dot{\theta}_0, \ddot{\theta}_0)$ is the terminal physical state of chunk $A$ at the seam instant, and $(\theta_1, \dot{\theta}_1, \ddot{\theta}_1)$ is the target state on incoming chunk $B$ at $t = T_{\mathrm{blend}}$. Matching six boundary conditions requires six independent coefficients ($a_0 \dots a_5$), uniquely dictating a fifth-degree polynomial:
$$\theta(t) = a_0 + a_1 t + a_2 t^2 + a_3 t^3 + a_4 t^4 + a_5 t^5$$

Evaluating boundary conditions at $t = 0$ directly yields the first three coefficients: $a_0 = \theta_0$, $a_1 = \dot{\theta}_0$, and $a_2 = \frac{1}{2}\ddot{\theta}_0$. The remaining three coefficients $[a_3, a_4, a_5]^\top$ satisfy the $3 \times 3$ linear system evaluated at duration $T = T_{\mathrm{blend}}$:[^fn-math-quintic-solve]

$$\begin{bmatrix} T^3 & T^4 & T^5 \\ 3T^2 & 4T^3 & 5T^4 \\ 6T & 12T^2 & 20T^3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a_3 \\ a_4 \\ a_5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \theta_1 - \left(\theta_0 + \dot{\theta}_0 T + \frac{1}{2}\ddot{\theta}_0 T^2\right) \\ \dot{\theta}_1 - \left(\dot{\theta}_0 + \ddot{\theta}_0 T\right) \\ \ddot{\theta}_1 - \ddot{\theta}_0 \end{bmatrix}$$ {#eq-plan-quintic-spline-matrix}

[^fn-math-quintic-solve]: **Closed-form quintic spline inversion**: Because the $3 \times 3$ coefficient matrix in @eq-plan-quintic-spline-matrix is constant for a chosen transition horizon $T$, inverting it symbolically yields explicit scalar formulas for $a_3, a_4, a_5$ that a microcontroller can evaluate without numerical matrix factorization; execution time must be measured on the selected controller; see @sec-appendix-control-splines for the algebraic expansion.

Inverting @eq-plan-quintic-spline-matrix yields closed-form algebraic expressions (@sec-appendix-control-splines) with fixed work per joint; this arithmetic complexity does not specify measured execution time. Differentiating $\theta(t)$ three times gives the commanded jerk:

$$j(t) = \dddot{\theta}(t) = 6 a_3 + 24 a_4 t + 60 a_5 t^2$$ {#eq-plan-quintic-jerk}

Because $j(t)$ in @eq-plan-quintic-jerk is quadratic in time, its extrema over $[0, T]$ occur strictly at the boundaries ($t = 0$ or $t = T$) or at the single interior stationary point $t^* = -a_4 / (5 a_5)$ (when $a_5\ne0$ and $t^* \in (0, T)$). If $a_5=0$, jerk is linear or constant and its endpoint values suffice. The safety microcontroller can therefore evaluate the exact peak jerk $|j_{\text{peak}}|$ analytically without numerical line searches. The same holds for each joint's other derivatives. Acceleration extrema lie at the roots of the quadratic jerk and velocity extrema at the roots of the cubic acceleration, both in closed form. Coupled joint torque is different. Along a polynomial $\mathbf{q}(t)$, the right-hand side of @eq-plan-rigidbody-dynamics is not a polynomial, because $\mathbf{M}$, $\mathbf{C}$, and $\mathbf{g}$ depend on $\mathbf{q}$ through sines and cosines, so its peak has no closed form. The checker evaluates torque at samples and bounds its variation between them, the same argument @sec-planning-intrasample-overshoot applies to velocity.

The physical consequence of bounded jerk directly governs actuator health, inverter voltage headroom, and transmission life. When a trajectory generator specifies motion using time-parameterized polynomials or spline collocations, it converts discrete kinematic targets into continuous functions whose derivatives map directly to the electrical and mechanical states of the actuator. In permanent-magnet synchronous motors (PMSM) governed by Field-Oriented Control (FOC), joint torque rate couples directly to jerk via $\dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}}(t) = \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q}) \dddot{\mathbf{q}}(t) + \dot{\mathbf{M}}(\mathbf{q}) \ddot{\mathbf{q}}(t) + \dots$. For a single joint under rigid effective inertia $J_{\text{eff}} = J_L + N_g^2 J_{\text{rotor}}$, the torque rate is $\dot{\tau} = J_{\text{eff}} j(t)$. Using a joint-effective torque constant $K_t$ so that output torque satisfies $\tau = K_t I_q$, commanding a torque rate $\dot{\tau}$ requires a proportional stator current slew rate:

$$\frac{dI_q}{dt} = \frac{J_{\text{eff}}}{K_t} j(t)$$

Here $K_t$ includes gear ratio and the applicable transmission efficiency; substituting a motor-side constant directly would mix output inertia with motor torque. Motor winding inductance $L$ and available voltage limit current slew. A loose necessary screen for a positive motoring segment, with positive resistive and back-EMF drops, is:

$$V_{\mathrm{bus}} \ge L \frac{dI_q}{dt} + R I_q + K_b \omega$$ {#eq-plan-inverter-headroom}

In @eq-plan-inverter-headroom, $R$ is winding resistance, $K_b$ is the motor back-EMF constant, and $\omega$ is motor speed. The usable $q$-axis voltage is only a modulation-dependent fraction of the DC bus. The actual feasibility check must use that available voltage and the signed, coupled motor equations, including regeneration; the scalar screen is not sufficient inverter qualification.

An acceleration discontinuity asks the reference model for an instantaneous torque and current step. Finite voltage and winding inductance prevent the drive from delivering that step exactly. The resulting tracking error, saturation, and protection response depend on the configured drive and load; an ideal unbounded jerk demand alone does not prove an overcurrent trip. The bridge must therefore satisfy both the reference derivatives and the measured actuator response.

Parameterizing a transition as a quintic bridge supplies enough coefficients to match position, velocity, and acceleration at both ends. That construction removes acceleration steps, but it does not establish that the interior jerk, torque, or required current slew fits the actuator. The checker evaluates the per-joint extrema from @eq-plan-quintic-jerk against the drive constraints in @eq-plan-inverter-headroom, checks the sampled coupled torque with its inter-sample bound, and rejects a bridge that fails either. A fixed-degree polynomial can be evaluated with bounded work per axis on a chosen controller. Coefficient synthesis and whole-trajectory extrema checks occur before dispatch, with earlier admission checking the reachable seam envelope; the measured worst-case execution time, including memory access and monitoring, must fit the configured deadline.

A local quintic bridge makes seam matching explicit. A global representation can offer different checking shortcuts. **Uniform B-splines** parameterize trajectories as $\mathbf{q}(t) = \sum_{i=0}^m \mathbf{p}_i B_{i, p}(t)$, where $\mathbf{p}_i$ are control points, $B_{i,p}$ are basis functions of degree $p$, and $u_i$ below denote knot times. With simple knots, these splines have $C^{p-1}$ continuity. Their **convex hull property** contains the curve within the hull of its control points, allowing collision checkers to prune spatial evaluations. Differentiation gives control points $\mathbf{v}_i = \frac{p}{u_{i+p+1}-u_{i+1}}(\mathbf{p}_{i+1} - \mathbf{p}_i)$ for the derivative spline, so control-point differences can bound velocity and higher derivatives. Those bounds do not remove actuator or clearance checks. For streaming replacements, the representation must also permit a checked join within the admission deadline.

@Tbl-11-trajectory-representations separates the continuity supplied by each representation from the dynamic checks still required before execution.

| Representation                       | Native seam property                                                                                                                 | Checks before execution                                                                                                                      |
|:-------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Cubic polynomial ($C^1$)             | Matches $q, \dot{q}$; adjoining acceleration need not match.                                                                         | Check acceleration matching and interior limits; position and velocity matching alone are insufficient.                                      |
| Quintic bridge ($C^2$)               | Matches $q,\dot q,\ddot q$ at both ends; jerk is quadratic within each bridge.                                                       | Check interior extrema, torque rates, inverter headroom, and clearance.                                                                      |
| Septic polynomial ($C^3$)            | Can match derivatives through jerk at both endpoints.                                                                                | Check interior derivatives and actuator limits; endpoint matching does not bound their magnitudes.                                           |
| Uniform B-spline (degree $p$)        | $C^{p-1}$ continuity; convex hull bounds spatial curve.                                                                              | Constrain control point differences for velocity/jerk; check global knot system.                                                             |
| Neural action chunk (ACT, Diffusion) | Discrete samples; continuity depends on interpolation and seam constraints.                                                          | Project onto feasibility manifold via numerical solver or $C^2$ quintic bridge; latch stop.                                                  |
| Online jerk-limited generator        | Reaches a target $(q,\dot q,\ddot q)$ from any current state within per-axis $v$, $a$, $j$ bounds; the generator picks the duration. | Check coupled torque, clearance, evidence age, and the configured limits themselves; kinematic feasibility by construction is not admission. |

: **Trajectory representations and required checks**: Smooth parameterization helps form a candidate but does not by itself prove dynamic feasibility. {#tbl-11-trajectory-representations tbl-colwidths="[24,36,40]"}

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-seam-reflected-inertia
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_torque, fmt_multiple, fmt_angular_velocity, fmt_inertia, fmt_latency, check

class PlanningSeamInertia:
    """Illustrative one-tick velocity request vs. symmetric C2 blend."""

    joint = (
        Actuators.PandaClassJoint.CSG_25_50_ILM70x18
    )  # category: datasheet; CSG-25-50 gear ratio and torque limits, ILM 70x18 rotor plus gear input inertia
    j_reflected = joint.reflected_inertia  # category: derived; N^2 J_rotor, 0.1835 kg m^2
    delta_omega = 0.2 * ureg.radian / second  # category: illustrative; reference velocity gap
    dt_tick = 1 * millisecond  # category: chosen; servo tick
    t_blend = 50 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; blend duration
    tau_step = calc_seam_acceleration_torque_jump(joint.gear_ratio, joint.rotor_inertia, (delta_omega / dt_tick).to(ureg.radian / second**2))
    tau_blend_mean = calc_seam_acceleration_torque_jump(joint.gear_ratio, joint.rotor_inertia, (delta_omega / t_blend).to(ureg.radian / second**2))
    # Symmetric C2 velocity blend: a(u)=6*delta_omega*u*(1-u)/T.
    tau_blend_peak = 1.5 * tau_blend_mean
    peak_reduction = tau_step / tau_blend_peak
    tau_rated = joint.rated_torque  # category: datasheet; L10 rated torque
    tau_peak_rated = joint.peak_torque  # category: datasheet; repeated peak torque
    # One-tick velocity change the whole repeated peak could supply to reflected rotor inertia alone.
    dq_ceiling = (tau_peak_rated * dt_tick / j_reflected).to(ureg.radian / second)
    check(abs(tau_step.magnitude - 36.7) < 0.01, "one-tick request changed")
    check(abs(tau_blend_mean.magnitude - 0.734) < 0.001, "blend mean changed")
    check(abs(tau_blend_peak.magnitude - 1.101) < 0.001, "blend peak changed")
    check(abs(peak_reduction.magnitude - 50 / 1.5) < 0.01, "peak ratio changed")
    check(abs(dq_ceiling.magnitude - 0.6921) < 1e-4, "one-tick velocity ceiling changed")
    check(delta_omega < dq_ceiling, "notebook velocity gap no longer below the one-tick ceiling")
    check(tau_step < tau_rated, "one-tick request no longer below the rated torque")
    tau_step_str = fmt_torque(tau_step, precision=1)
    tau_mean_str = fmt_torque(tau_blend_mean, precision=2)
    tau_peak_str = fmt_torque(tau_blend_peak, precision=1)
    reduction_mult_str = fmt_multiple(peak_reduction.magnitude, precision=1)
    j_reflected_str = fmt_inertia(j_reflected, precision=2)
    tau_rated_str = fmt_torque(tau_rated, precision=0)
    tau_peak_rated_str = fmt_torque(tau_peak_rated, precision=0)
    dt_tick_str = fmt_latency(dt_tick, unit=millisecond)
    dq_ceiling_str = fmt_angular_velocity(dq_ceiling, precision=2)
    delta_omega_str = fmt_angular_velocity(delta_omega, precision=1)
    t_blend_str = fmt_latency(t_blend, unit=millisecond)
```

::: {#nbk-planning-seam-acceleration-jump-reflected-inertia-torque .callout-notebook title="Seam acceleration and torque requests"}
For a Panda-class strain-wave joint, a CSG-25-50 gear driven by a TQ-RoboDrive ILM 70x18 motor (Franka does not publish the Panda's joint internals, so the example pairs published parts of that torque class), reflected rotor inertia is `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.j_reflected_str`. Correcting a `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.delta_omega_str` reference velocity gap in one `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.dt_tick_str` tick asks for `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_step_str` of inertial torque. Datasheet ratings give `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_rated_str` rated continuous and `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_rated_str` repeated peak torque; this one-tick **request** falls below the rated limit. A symmetric $C^2$ velocity blend over `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.t_blend_str` has `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_mean_str` mean and `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_str` peak inertial torque, a `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.reduction_mult_str` peak-request reduction. Total torque still includes load, gravity, friction, and control response; it needs a full peak and thermal check.
